title: Heedlessness, the forgetting
hookLine: forgetting Allah in the rush of the day

cards: Car. Meeting. Lunch at the desk.
Phone. Sleep. Nothing in that day was wrong.

teach.b: Start with a verse that names the cure and the disease together.

The Qur'an tells the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, to remember his Lord within himself, humbly and with awe, at morning and evening, and it ends, in Pickthall's words: "And be not thou of the neglectful."
The Arabic word there is al-ghafilin, the heedless. Morning and evening: the edges of the day, the very times a rush begins and ends. Second, what forgetting does.
Another verse warns against being like those who forgot Allah, so that he made them forget themselves. Forgetting Allah isn't a small gap on a schedule; it comes with losing track of your own soul.
Third, a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari puts it starkly: the one who remembers his Lord and the one who doesn't are like the living and the dead. Not good and bad. Awake and not.
And last, the cure, which you first met as the heart's polish on day three hundred eight. Heedlessness isn't fixed by one long session.
It's fixed by small bells through the day: the call to prayer, the words said on waking, before eating, on leaving the house. Each one is a tap on the shoulder, for a day that, left alone, forgets.

how: Muslims counter ghaflah, heedlessness, with dhikr, the remembrance of Allah, built into the day through the prayers, the call to prayer, and short remembrances said on waking, eating and leaving home.

o: a big sin someone sets out to commit on purpose
being tired or sleepy during the prayer itself
forgetting Allah in the ordinary rush of a day

games.q: heedlessness, the forgetting — tap the pairs.
p: one who remembers and one who doesn't

s: heedlessness is a sin someone sets out to commit
it's a remembering that gets skipped, often in a day where nothing else went wrong.
a hadith in al-Bukhari compares the one who remembers and the one who doesn't to the living and the dead
the verse in al-A'raf places remembering at morning and evening
and ends: "And be not thou of the neglectful."

games.q: you've gone a whole busy day without a single thought of Allah. what does today's teaching offer as the cure?
o: one long session to make up for it.
small reminders spread through the day.
nothing: busy days are just like that.
games.why: heedlessness is answered the way sleep is interrupted: by small bells through the day, like the call to prayer and short remembrances.

practice: Picture the busiest part of today and give it a small reminder, a phone alarm or a sticky note, with one word on it: Allah, or wake up, or something you're grateful for.
Decide what you'll do when it comes: one breath, one line of a remembrance you already know, one look out a window. If you pray, you can ask not to be among the heedless.

wordCard.voice: Ghaflah. Heedlessness: forgetting Allah in the rush of the day; in the Qur'an, the neglectful. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: heedlessness, neglectful forgetting; the Qur'an speaks of al-ghafilin, the heedless.

carryVoice: Your line: wake up. The living and the dead, the hadith says: awake and not. Tomorrow, the last disease of the heart: despair.

sources.q: And be not thou of the neglectful.
